Topics Countries Explainer About Contributors The Quarterly Submissions Search Economics Trade diversification won’t fix Vietnam’s import dependence Published: 24 October 2026 Reading Time: 5 mins Back Authors Guanie Lim National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies Nhat Anh Nguyen Independent Back In Brief Vietnam’s push to diversify trade through deeper ties with Australia, New Zealand and other partners does not resolve its core vulnerability of weak domestic firm capability. Despite new trade agreements and rising trade, Vietnam remains heavily dependent on China and South Korea for inputs. Recent government resolutions aim to strengthen private-sector capacity and localisation, helping to transform Vietnam’s global integration into greater domestic value-adding capabilities.
Listen to this article In August 2026, Vietnam’s President To Lam and several high-ranking ministers visited Australia and New Zealand, reaching a broad consensus with their counterparts in both countries on strengthening cooperation on defence and security, science and technology, as well as trade and investment . This reflects Vietnam’s push to diversify trade and break away from trade dependencies. But the benefits of trade diversification are limited if Vietnam cannot translate bilateral trade into meaningful value added.
One of the more significant developments were the meetings between Vietnam’s Acting Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung and his Australian and New Zealand counterparts. Australian Minister for Trade and Tourism Don Farrell pledged to continue working towards raising bilateral trade with Vietnam to US$20 billion , while New Zealand’s Minister for Trade and Investment Todd McClay agreed to ramp up efforts to achieve the countries’ existing target of US$3 billion .
It is prudent for Vietnam to increase bilateral trade with Australia and New Zealand. Trade exchanges capitalise on both the complementary nature of both countries’ economies — Australian critical minerals and New Zealand’s agri-food exports feeding Vietnam’s manufacturing and food-security needs — and existing cooperation frameworks. And they can also reduce Vietnamese reliance on China and the United States, which are by far its two largest trade partners, lowering Vietnam’s exposure to shocks in either relationship. Still, even if the combined trade pledges are achieved, the amount will still be a fraction of Vietnam’s total trade portfolio.
In 2025, bilateral trade with China amounted to US$256.4 billion, while trade with the United States came to US$172.5 billion . China has served as the largest supplier to Vietnam for years, while the US has consistently kept its position as Vietnam’s largest export market.
That does not make Hanoi’s diversification efforts misguided — they are necessary, but not sufficient. Besides Australia and New Zealand, Vietnam has actively courted various trade partners and signed economic partnership agreements. To Lam’s May 2026 visits to India and Singapore produced new commitments on trade, investment, technology and energy, while Vietnam secured a Comprehensive Partnership with the United Arab Emirates in 2024 . Vietnam has also channelled considerable energy into modern industries like semiconductor manufacturing and fintech.
Each deal widens the menu of markets and standards Vietnamese firms could, in principle, sell into. But a government signature on a partnership agreement is not a firm capability. Diversification at the level of policy does not automatically become diversification at the level of firms and production networks and absent that second, harder shift broader trade is unlikely to reduce dependence.
Vietnam has pursued diversification with South Korea, rapidly increasing imports since the early 2010s , making it Vietnam’s second largest import source since 2013. South Korean firms such as Samsung are also some of Vietnam’s largest foreign investors. But rather than reducing Vietnam’s dependence on imported inputs, this South Korean-centric value chain has locked Vietnam into a new ‘ Pacific Trade Triangle ’ with China, South Korea and the United States, deepening its dependence on China and South Korea for intermediate and capital goods. Rising imports from China, and to a lesser extent South Korea, have closely mirrored increasing US exports.
But the real constraint underlying Vietnam’s trade dependence may be the limited capability of its domestic firms, rather than its number of trade partners. One giveaway is Vietnam’s Incremental Capital-Output Ratio , a measure of how much investment it takes to generate one extra unit of growth, which rose from 7.6 in 2016‒2020 to 8.5 in 2021‒2024 . Vietnam’s ratio is also consistently more volatile and higher than its regional peers . The extra output that generally comes with more investment has remained subdued.
But if capital has been allocated sub-optimally, the answer is better intermediation and capability building — without which Vietnamese firms stay dependent on imported inputs rather than developing their own. So Resolution 68, issued by the Vietnamese government on 4 May 2025, might prove one of the most consequential pieces of the development puzzle .
The resolution aims to position the private sector as the locomotive of the economy, prioritising efforts to improve access to capital and strengthen links with transnational corporations. This agenda was reinforced by a resolution on its foreign investment strategy in June 2026. The resolution seeks to raise localisation rates to 45–50 per cent in key industries, develop around 10,000 domestic firms in foreign direct investment supply chains — including 500–1000 Tier-1 suppliers — and require 75 per cent of new foreign direct investment to come from developed, technologically advanced economies.
The resolutions address a challenge that cannot be met solely through trade diplomacy — how to turn Vietnam’s global integration into stronger domestic productive know-how. This is not to say trade diversification is meaningless. Done well, it can widen access to technologies, though the evidence suggests this mainly holds where firms already have the capacity to absorb and adapt new knowledge — precisely the gap Resolutions 68 and 10 are trying to close.
Yet diversifying export markets without fixing domestic skills development simply spreads the underlying inefficiency across even more partners. The real test is not so much which flags appear on Vietnamese trade statistics in the next few months. Instead, what matters is whether Vietnamese firms continue to perform relatively low value-added tasks in three or four years’ time.
Guanie Lim is Associate Professor at the National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies, Japan.
Nhat Anh Nguyen is an Independent Researcher based in Hanoi, Vietnam .
